name: Relationship Prioritization
contentMarkdown:
# Relationship Prioritization

Relationship prioritization is the ORCA activity of deciding which connections between objects deserve support in the product and prominence in its interface. It helps teams turn a relationship model into a manageable scope and useful paths through information.

A connection can exist in the data model without needing a visible navigation link in every view. Decide what people need to understand, reach, or manage in each context.

## What are you prioritizing?

A [Nested Object Matrix](/glossary/nested-object-matrix.html) helps discover possible connections. Relationship requirements describe how a connection works, including its mechanics and cardinality.

Prioritization asks which capabilities and paths matter for the intended release. A navigation design then determines how those chosen paths appear.

## Example: managing a travel booking

A first release supports agents working on trips and their bookings.

| Connection | Example decision | User need |
|---|---|---|
| Trip to Bookings | Show related bookings and a way to add one | Manage the trip's travel services. |
| Booking to Trip | Provide a contextual route back to the trip | Understand the record after entering through search. |
| Trip to Travelers | Show associated travelers | Verify whom the trip concerns. |
| Traveler to all Trips | Support if cross-trip history is part of the release | Investigate earlier travel without duplicate searches. |
| Booking to Supplier profile | Defer the profile route if supplier management is out of scope | Retain the supplier information needed for the booking. |

Deferring a supplier profile does not remove the need to identify the supplier. Record where that information comes from and how agents use it.

## How to choose

Start with representative tasks and entry points. Evaluate the need in both directions: a person viewing a Trip may need its Bookings, while someone opening a Booking directly needs its Trip context.

Consider related-record volume, permissions, maintenance cost, and what happens when no related record exists. Document deferred capabilities and the evidence that would make them necessary.

Avoid removing a relationship merely because its interface is inconvenient. A required business connection still needs an appropriate representation.

## How to test it

Ask users to complete a routine task and investigate an exception. Start one task from search or a notification.

Observe whether users find the next relevant record, understand where they arrived, and retain enough context to return. Review the result before adding more links.

## Related terms

- [Nested Object Matrix](/glossary/nested-object-matrix.html)
- [ORCA Relationship Requirements](/glossary/orca-relationship-requirements.html)
- [Structural Navigation Model](/glossary/structural-navigation-model.html)
- [Object Prioritization](/glossary/object-prioritization.html)

## Sources

- [The UX Level-Up: Relationship Prioritization with Jake Zukowski](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/077-orca-series-10-from-inheriting-strategy-to-shaping/id1531717094?i=1000723486950)

name: Attribute Prioritization
contentMarkdown:
# Attribute Prioritization

Attribute prioritization is the ORCA activity of deciding which information about an object matters most for a release and for the views people use. It helps teams choose what to show prominently, what to reveal in detail, and what can wait.

The priority depends on the user's task and context. Information needed to choose a record in search can differ from information needed to edit it or resolve an exception.

## Two decisions to separate

First decide which attributes the product needs to support its intended work. Then decide how prominently to present the supported attributes in each view.

A supplier confirmation number might be essential data even when a compact queue usually shows only a booking reference, status, and service date. Removing it from that queue does not mean removing it from the model.

## Example: prioritizing Booking information

Suppose an agent scans a queue for bookings awaiting supplier confirmation.

| Attribute | Queue treatment | Detail treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Booking reference | Always visible for identification | Same reference in the heading. |
| Status | Visible and filterable | Include relevant status history. |
| Service date | Visible to assess urgency | Show complete dates and times as needed. |
| Supplier confirmation number | Show when relevant to the queue's task | Show when available; explain a meaningful absence. |
| Internal notes | Avoid displaying a long note in every row | Make permitted notes available for investigation. |

This is a task-specific example. A queue for reconciling supplier records could need different fields.

## How to make the decision

Ask which attributes help users identify the object, compare candidates, choose an action, or recognize an exception. Use observed tasks and actual records when discussing tradeoffs with stakeholders.

Check both routine and unusual cases. A rare field may become the most important information during an urgent exception. Decide how users reach it when needed.

Record the reason for a priority and where it applies. This gives future reviewers a basis for changing the design when the workflow changes.

## How to test the result

Give users a realistic queue and a task such as finding the booking that needs attention next. Observe what they inspect and whether important information forces repeated navigation.

Check long values, missing data, narrow screens, and keyboard access. Progressive disclosure should keep necessary information discoverable at the moment it matters.

## Related terms

- [Object Attributes in OOUX](/glossary/object-attributes-ooux.html)
- [Object Prioritization](/glossary/object-prioritization.html)
- [Object Representation](/glossary/object-representation-ooux.html)
- [Progressive Disclosure](/glossary/progressive-disclosure.html)

## Sources

- [The UX Level-Up: Attribute Prioritization with Jake Zukowski](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/082-orca-series-12-building-trust-through-attributes/id1531717094?i=1000733396352)

name: CTA Prioritization
contentMarkdown:
# CTA Prioritization

CTA prioritization is the ORCA activity of deciding which actions on an object the product should support and how prominently to present them. It connects release scope and interface emphasis to user needs, business goals, and the context in which an action becomes relevant.

A CTA can become a button, link, menu item, or entry into a longer interaction. Giving an action visual prominence is one implementation decision within that larger assessment.

## Start with the action's purpose

Use the [CTA Matrix](/glossary/cta-matrix.html) to identify candidate actions by object and role. Develop the reason and conditions for each action before deciding its position.

An action can be important despite being infrequent. For example, resolving an urgent booking issue may matter more in that moment than the queue's most common operation.

## Example: actions on a confirmed Booking

An illustrative travel operations product supports these actions for an assigned agent:

| Action | Priority decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| View fare conditions | Easy to find near booking details | Helps the agent assess available changes. |
| Request cancellation | Clearly available when eligible | Supports a specific task with consequential effects. |
| Update internal note | Secondary action | Useful supporting work, with lower emphasis in this view. |
| Export record | Available in a labeled menu | Occasional task that does not need to dominate the page. |
| Delete booking | Excluded from this release | The agreed workflow preserves booking history. |

These choices apply to the example's workflow. They do not establish a universal button hierarchy.

## Keep availability and prominence distinct

An eligible cancellation action can deserve clear placement while still requiring review of the target and consequences. A pending request needs a way to inspect its progress.

If an action is unavailable, decide whether showing the reason will help the user continue. Apply the underlying permission and eligibility rules when the request executes.

User goals such as canceling, declining, or leaving a service also need understandable paths. Commercial preference alone is a poor basis for making a legitimate task difficult to find.

## Validate the choice

Test whether users find the action they need, understand its label, and anticipate its result. Include different roles and object states.

Review misclicks and incomplete tasks alongside completion. A prominent control that attracts clicks without producing the intended outcome needs further investigation.

## Related terms

- [CTA Matrix](/glossary/cta-matrix.html)
- [Object-Oriented User Stories](/glossary/object-oriented-user-stories.html)
- [Attribute Prioritization](/glossary/attribute-prioritization.html)
- [State Transition Matrix](/glossary/state-transition-matrix.html)

## Sources

- [The UX Level-Up: CTA Prioritization with Jake Zukowski](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/079-orca-series-11-ctas-that-align-teams-and-earn/id1531717094?i=1000725166619)

name: Shapeshifter Matrix
contentMarkdown:
# Shapeshifter Matrix

A Shapeshifter Matrix is an OOUX tool for examining the different representations and variants of an object. It helps teams make differences intentional while preserving the cues people need to recognize the object across an interface.

An object can legitimately appear as a compact search result, a row in a work queue, and a detailed record. Problems arise when unexplained changes make it difficult to identify the same thing or understand its available actions.

## What should the matrix compare?

Start with the contexts in which the object appears. Record the information shown, relevant role or state, available actions, and the reason for a difference.

The table below is one lightweight format. It is an illustrative working artifact, rather than a prescribed official template.

## Example: Booking B-52 across views

In this example, the booking is Awaiting confirmation. An assigned agent can update permitted details; a support reviewer has read access.

| Representation | Identifying information | Actions and rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Search result | Booking reference, service date, status | Open the record; enough detail to choose the right match. |
| Trip booking row | Same reference and status, supplier name | Open details within the trip context. |
| Agent detail view | Same identity cues, full permitted booking data | Edit eligible fields; manage the booking within the agent's authority. |
| Reviewer detail view | Same identity cues, permitted review data | Inspect history; editing is unavailable for this role. |

The role difference changes available actions. It should not make the status mean something different.

## How to use it

Choose one real record and follow it through the views. List differences before deciding which to keep. For each difference, identify the task, permission, or space constraint it serves.

Then check other important states. A canceled booking may need a cancellation date; a draft may lack a supplier confirmation number. Capture these conditions without creating a separate component for every possible combination.

## What should remain consistent?

Define recognizable labels, reference formatting, status meaning, and the relationship between an action and its result. Layout and detail can vary with context.

Test whether users recognize the booking after moving between views and whether they understand the role-dependent controls. Also check accessible names and keyboard operation in each representation. A consistent screenshot alone cannot establish consistent behavior.

## Related terms

- [Four UX Fails in OOUX](/glossary/ooux-ux-fails.html)
- [Object Representation](/glossary/object-representation-ooux.html)
- [Interaction Invariant](/glossary/interaction-invariant.html)
- [Attribute Prioritization](/glossary/attribute-prioritization.html)

name: Tree Systems in OOUX
contentMarkdown:
# Tree Systems in OOUX

A Tree System in OOUX is a pattern of related object types that move from a general concept toward more specific, contextual forms. It includes a root, a more specific “fruit” object, and sometimes intermediate “branch” objects.

The term comes from the OOUX community. It describes a modeling pattern, with roots and fruit used as explanatory metaphors.

## Example: a course and its scheduled sessions

Consider an illustrative training product:

| Object type | Example instance | Information owned at this level |
|---|---|---|
| Course | First Aid Basics | Shared learning objectives and standard description. |
| Course Offering | First Aid Basics at East Center | Local delivery details and contact information. |
| Scheduled Session | That offering on June 12 at 10 a.m. | Start time, capacity, and remaining places. |

A learner can read the course description before choosing a location and session. Registering requires a specific Scheduled Session.

Each row describes a different object type with its own instances. A scheduled session is not simply another Course instance. Its structure and available actions differ.

## Where should information belong?

Store shared learning objectives on Course and reference them where needed. Store session capacity on Scheduled Session because it applies to that occurrence.

For this product, the team might let central staff edit the standard description and local staff manage session capacity. Those permissions are example decisions to validate.

When shared information changes, decide how it should appear in existing offerings and historical sessions. Some records may need a snapshot rather than the latest description.

## Tree Systems, hierarchy, and inheritance

A hierarchy alone does not establish a Tree System. A category containing articles, each with comments, does not automatically express increasing specificity of one concept.

Inheritance concerns types sharing a common structure or behavior. A Tree System connects contextual forms that can have different information and actions. A [junction object](/glossary/junction-object.html) may participate in the pattern when a connection needs its own attributes.

## How to check the model

Ask users which thing they are viewing, selecting, editing, and registering for. Test two locations and several sessions for the same course.

Check that an edit to one session's capacity affects the intended record, while shared course information remains consistent wherever the product is meant to reuse it.

## Related terms

- [Junction Object](/glossary/junction-object.html)
- [Object Inheritance in OOUX](/glossary/object-inheritance-ooux.html)
- [Object Attributes in OOUX](/glossary/object-attributes-ooux.html)
- [Conceptual Schema](/glossary/conceptual-schema.html)

## Sources
